Rust's regex crate compiles and reuses regexes through `Regex::new()` for one-off matches, or via `LazyLock`, `once_cell`, or the `regex!` macro for reusing the same compiled pattern across multiple searches. The crate does not support lookahead, lookbehind (look-around), and backreferences, trading those features for guaranteed linear-time O(m*n) matching performance.

## Compiling and Reusing Regexes

- Use [`Regex::new(pattern)`](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/struct.Regex.html#method.new) to compile a pattern, which is expensive (microseconds to milliseconds depending on size), so compile once and reuse the `Regex` value ([Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/strings-text/regex/)).
- Use [`std::sync::LazyLock`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.LazyLock.html) or the `once_cell` crate to store a static regex that is compiled on first use and reused thereafter ([docs.rs/regex](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#avoid-re-compiling-regexes-especially-in-a-loop)).
- Use the [`regex!` macro](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/macro.regex.html) for compile-time or lazy static compilation inside functions ([docs.rs/regex](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#example-find-a-middle-initial)).
- Use [`RegexBuilder`](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/struct.RegexBuilder.html) to configure options like case insensitivity before compilation ([docs.rs/regex](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#overview)).

## Unsupported Regex Features

- Look-around assertions (lookahead and lookbehind) are not supported ([docs.rs/regex](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- Backreferences (e.g., `\1`, `\2`) are not supported ([docs.rs/regex](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/)).
- For features beyond the crate's scope, the [`fancy-regex` crate](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#alternatives) adds lookahead and lookbehind support, though at the cost of linear-time guarantees ([Rust SME Cookbook](https://rust.codeguides.io/strings-text/regex/)).

Rayon provides parallel iterators that work like standard Rust iterators but execute in parallel across multiple threads. To use them, import the prelude and call `par_iter()`, `par_iter_mut()`, or `into_par_iter()` on collections, then chain operations like `map()`, `filter()`, and `reduce()` ([rayon::iter module](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/iter/)).

## Creating and using parallel iterators

- Convert any iterable to a parallel iterator with `par_iter()` for immutable access, `par_iter_mut()` for mutable access, or `into_par_iter()` to consume the collection ([rayon::iter module](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/iter/)).
- Chain operations like `map()`, `filter()`, `fold()`, and `reduce()` to transform and aggregate data in parallel ([ParallelIterator trait](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html)). Example: `input.par_iter().map(|i| i * i).sum()` computes the sum of squares in parallel.
- Use `for_each()` to perform side effects on each element in parallel, or `for_each_with()` and `for_each_init()` to maintain thread-local state ([ParallelIterator trait](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html)).

## Controlling the global thread pool

- Call `rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder::new().num_threads(N).build_global().unwrap()` early in your program to set the number of threads in the global thread pool ([ThreadPoolBuilder](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)).
- If you don't call `build_global()`, the global thread pool automatically initializes with the number of threads determined by the `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` environment variable or the number of logical CPUs ([ThreadPoolBuilder](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)).
- Global thread pool initialization happens exactly once; calling `build_global()` a second time returns an error ([ThreadPoolBuilder](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)).

## Creating custom thread pools

- Build a custom thread pool with `rayon::ThreadPoolBuilder::new().num_threads(8).build().unwrap()` and execute code within it using `pool.install(|| { /* parallel code */ })` ([ThreadPoolBuilder](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)).
- Any parallel iterators or rayon operations called inside `install()` will execute within that custom thread pool, not the global pool ([ThreadPool](https://docs.rs/rayon/latest/rayon/struct.ThreadPool.html)).

The `tracing` crate uses macros to record spans and events, and subscribers are installed globally or locally in executables using the `tracing-subscriber` crate.

## Recording Spans

- Use the [`#[instrument]`](https://docs.rs/tracing-attributes/latest/tracing_attributes/attr.instrument.html) attribute on functions to automatically create and enter a span named after the function with parameters recorded as fields ([Overview · tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)).
- For asynchronous code, use the [`Future::instrument`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/trait.Instrument.html#method.instrument) combinator or the `#[instrument]` attribute to avoid span lifetime issues across await points ([Application level tracing for Rust](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing)).

## Recording Events

- Specify a log level and optional fields in the form `field_name = field_value`, separated by commas ([Overview · tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)).
- Include a formatted message after the fields, which creates an implicit `message` field ([Overview · tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)).

## Installing a Subscriber in Executables

- For more control, build a subscriber using `tracing_subscriber::fmt()` with methods like `.with_max_level()`, call `.finish()` to build it, and then either set it globally with [`set_global_default()`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html) or use [`with_default()`](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/subscriber/fn.with_default.html) to apply it locally within a closure ([Overview · tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)).
- Libraries should never call `set_global_default()`, as this will cause conflicts when executables try to set the default later ([Overview · tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/)).

- This allows code to distinguish timeout errors from user-initiated aborts, which produce `AbortError` instead.

Error E0382 occurs when you try to use a value after its ownership has been moved to another variable, which violates Rust's ownership system that ensures only one variable can own a resource at a time. [The official Rust documentation explains that "outside of workarounds like Rc, a value cannot be owned by more than one variable."](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)

## What Causes E0382

- **Move semantics on non-Copy types**: When you assign a non-Copy type (like `String`, `Vec`, or custom structs) to another variable, ownership transfers and the original variable becomes invalid. [Assignment moves non-Copy values because "Rust treats variables like physical objects. When you assign `let b = a`, you are handing the object from `a` to `b`. `a` no longer holds the object."](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-fix-rust-e0382-value-used-after-being-moved/)
- **Passing to functions**: Functions that take ownership (e.g., `fn takes_ownership(s: String)`) consume the value, leaving it inaccessible in the caller's scope.
- **Loop iterations**: [Iterating over owned values with `for s in v` moves each element, making the collection unavailable afterward.](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-25-fix-use-of-moved-value-rust/view)
- **Closures with move keyword**: The `move` keyword forces a closure to take ownership of captured variables.

## Fixes for E0382

- **Use references (borrowing)**: [Pass `&T` instead of `T` to let functions borrow without taking ownership; "using a reference, we can let another function borrow the value without changing its ownership."](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)
- **Clone the value**: [Call `.clone()` to create an independent copy when you genuinely need both the original and a separate instance, though "cloning is not free" and allocates new memory.](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/how-to-fix-rust-e0382-value-used-after-being-moved/)
- **Return ownership**: Have functions return the value back to transfer ownership back to the caller after processing.
- **Iterate by reference**: Use `&collection` or `.iter()` instead of consuming iterators to keep the collection accessible.
- **Use Copy types**: [Primitive types like `i32`, `bool`, and `f64` implement `Copy`, so assignment copies the bits and the original remains valid.](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-25-fix-use-of-moved-value-rust/view)
- **Use Rc/Arc for shared ownership**: [For single-threaded shared ownership use `Rc`, and for multi-threaded use `Arc`, which allow multiple variables to own the same data via reference counting.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0382.html)

Git's "refusing to merge unrelated histories" error occurs when you try to merge two branches or repositories that don't share a common ancestor commit in their history. Git prevents this by default as a safety feature to avoid accidentally combining unrelated projects.

## How to fix it

## Alternatives to consider

- If the branches are truly unrelated, consider whether keeping them in separate repositories makes more sense for your workflow ([unrelated-histories.md · GitHub](https://gist.github.com/kingluddite/7ec82fdfa3700427efa0e5b97196dea6)).

The ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error occurs when attempting to use CommonJS `require()` to import an ES module (ESM) package, which Node.js does not support because CommonJS uses synchronous loading while ES modules use asynchronous loading. - **Downgrade to a CommonJS version**: Install an older version of the problematic package built with CommonJS. This allows you to use the latest package versions but requires converting your entire codebase.
- **Use dynamic imports**: Replace static `require()` calls with dynamic `import()` in an async context ([DevGex](https://devgex.com/en/article/00021517)). This works in all Node.js versions 14+ but requires async/Promise handling.

## Current status

- The error remains relevant on all current Node.js versions because the underlying module system mismatch has not changed, and the ecosystem continues to see packages migrating to ESM-only releases. PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 23505 (unique_violation) means an INSERT or UPDATE tried to create a value that violates a unique constraint or primary key—the database rejected the write because that value already exists in a column or group of columns protected by uniqueness. [The error message names the specific constraint that rejected the write and includes a DETAIL line listing the conflicting column(s) and value](https://www.bytebase.com/reference/postgres/error/23505-duplicate-key-value/).

## Root causes and fixes

- **Sequence out of sync after bulk import**: After restoring data with explicit IDs or using `COPY`, the `SERIAL`/`IDENTITY` sequence falls behind the actual max ID in the table, so the next insert reuses an existing ID. [Reset the sequence to one above the maximum with `SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('table', 'id'), COALESCE((SELECT MAX(id) FROM table), 0) + 1, false);`](https://www.bytebase.com/reference/postgres/error/23505-duplicate-key-value/).
- **Non-atomic "find or create" code**: Patterns like Rails `find_or_create_by` or hand-rolled `SELECT then INSERT` race under concurrency—two requests both see "no match" and both try to insert, so the second fails. [Use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` to push the uniqueness check into a single atomic statement](https://www.bytebase.com/reference/postgres/error/23505-duplicate-key-value/).
- **Use ON CONFLICT for idempotent inserts**: When duplicate attempts are expected (webhook retries, job retries), use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (column) DO NOTHING` or `DO UPDATE` to handle collisions gracefully without failing. [For idempotency keys, treat 23505 as the success path for retries—don't log it as an error](https://www.bytebase.com/reference/postgres/error/23505-duplicate-key-value/).
- **Verify the constraint matches your data model**: [Before adding or changing a unique constraint, find existing duplicates and either merge rows or expand the constraint to include a scope column (e.g., `tenant_id`)](https://armordb.org/blog/fix-postgresql-duplicate-key-value).

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests indicates that the client has sent too many requests within a given timeframe; the server is asking you to slow down. This is a rate-limiting control signal, not a true error, and it's expected behavior when working with APIs.

## What 429 means

- [429 Too Many Requests on MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429) states: "This mechanism of asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called 'rate limiting'". Rate limiting restrictions may be server-wide, per resource, per IP address, per user, or based on authenticated credentials or cookies.

## How clients should respond

- **Check the Retry-After header**: [How to Handle HTTP 429 Responses on Throttle](https://throttle.com/guides/handle-http-429/) advises: "When Retry-After is valid, treat it as the earliest permitted retry time. A local backoff policy may choose a longer delay, but it should not choose a shorter one". The header can specify either a delay in seconds or an HTTP date string.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**: Implement capped exponential backoff (e.g., `delay = base * 2^attempt`) combined with random jitter to avoid the "thundering herd" problem where many clients retry simultaneously. [Handling HTTP 429 Too Many Requests on wtool.dev](https://wtool.dev/guides/http-429-rate-limiting-retry-after-backoff) explains: "When dozens or thousands of client instances hit a rate limit simultaneously and retry with a fixed delay, they will all synchronize their next requests. This creates massive traffic spikes, repeatedly crashing the server and locking all clients into continuous 429 loops".
- **Set retry limits and budgets**: [How to Handle HTTP 429 Responses on Throttle](https://throttle.com/guides/handle-http-429/) states: "Every retry policy needs a maximum delay, maximum attempt count, and total time budget. Without those boundaries, a retry loop can outlive the work it was meant to complete".
- **Make writes idempotent before retrying**: Never blindly retry non-idempotent operations like POST requests without an `Idempotency-Key` header to avoid duplicate transactions.
- **Queue non-urgent work**: [How to Handle HTTP 429 Responses on Throttle](https://throttle.com/guides/handle-http-429/) advises: "If work is not urgent, place it in a delayed queue and resume it after capacity returns".

Python's RecursionError occurs when a recursive function exceeds the interpreter's maximum call stack depth, typically triggered by missing base cases, incorrect recursive logic, or legitimately deep recursion. On September 21, 2026, the Rust Security Response Team announced that Miri was storing all environment variables—including secrets—to the `target/` directory, which when cached in GitHub Actions, could expose those secrets to pull requests ([GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/)).

## The vulnerability

- Miri saves environment variables to `target/` to retain build-relevant configuration between runs. GitHub Actions' caching allows PRs to read from caches written by main branch runs, enabling attackers to extract secrets via pull request CI. The issue is particularly dangerous because PR CI can be triggered by anyone with prior commit history on the repository ([Rust & AI Weekly #14](https://ddonprogramming.substack.com/p/rust-and-ai-weekly-14-miris-fix-leaves)).

## The fix and timeline

- Ralf Jung's patch merged on September 21 and shipped in the September 22 nightly. The fix restricts Miri to only preserving `CARGO_*` environment variables (excluding those ending in `_TOKEN`) and `OUT_DIR`, rather than the entire environment ([GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/)).

## How affected projects should respond

- Projects are vulnerable if they run `cargo miri` in CI with cached `target/` directories accessible to PRs and pass secrets as environment variables to that step. Immediate actions include upgrading to the September 22 nightly or later, disabling cache for Miri jobs, or scoping secrets away from those steps ([Rust & AI Weekly #14](https://ddonprogramming.substack.com/p/rust-and-ai-weekly-14-miris-fix-leaves)) (quote: "Upgrade the pinned nightly to a patched build. Keep secrets out of the Miri step, or disable caching for that job while correcting it"). After fixing the workflow, teams must clear affected caches and consider rotating any exposed credentials ([GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/)).

## Broader implications

- Even projects not running Miri should review whether jobs writing to public caches have access to secrets, as many build tools don't guarantee environment variables won't be stored in filesystem artifacts ([GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/09/21/github-actions-leaking-secrets-when-miri-output-is-cached/)).

To cross-compile a Rust binary for aarch64 Linux with cargo, add the target to your toolchain and pass the `--target` flag to cargo. The simplest approach requires just two steps: [adding the aarch64 target](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html) and telling cargo to build for that target.

## Basic setup

- Add the aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu target with `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([Cross-compilation · rustup](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/cross-compilation.html))
- Build with `cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html))
- Optionally set a default target in `.cargo/config.toml` under `[build] target = "aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu"` to avoid passing `--target` each time ([Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html))

## When linking or native dependencies are needed

- For Debian/Ubuntu systems, install the GCC cross-compiler and target libraries: `sudo apt install gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu libssl-dev:arm64`, then set `CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` ([Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html))
- Use `cross` (a drop-in cargo replacement) to avoid manual setup: `cargo install cross` then `cross build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([cross-rs/cross](https://github.com/cross-rs/cross))
- Alternatively use `cargo-zigbuild` with Zig's bundled compiler and sysroots: `cargo install cargo-zigbuild` then `cargo zigbuild --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html))

## Testing cross-compiled binaries

- Install QEMU userspace emulation to run tests: `sudo apt install qemu-user-binfmt`, then run `cargo test --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([Rust Project Primer](https://rustprojectprimer.com/building/cross.html))
- The `cross` tool includes QEMU inside its Docker containers, so testing works automatically with `cross test --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` ([cross-rs/cross](https://github.com/cross-rs/cross))

To squash the last 3 commits in git, use `git rebase -i HEAD~3` to open an interactive rebase editor, then change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) for the 2nd and 3rd commits, keep `pick` for the first commit, save the file, and optionally edit the combined commit message in the next editor that appears.

## Interactive Rebase Method

- Run `git rebase -i HEAD~3` to start interactive rebase on the last 3 commits ([Git Tools - Rewriting History](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History))
- In the editor, replace `pick` with `squash` (or `s`) for commits 2 and 3, leaving the first commit as `pick` ([Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/))
- Save and close the editor, then git will open another editor to combine the commit messages ([Git Squash Commits – Squashing the Last N Commits into One Commit](https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/git-squash-commits/))
- Edit or keep the combined message, save, and the squash is complete ([Git Tools - Rewriting History](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History))

## Important Caveat

- Only squash commits that haven't been pushed to a shared repository, as squashing rewrites history and will confuse other developers ([Git Tools - Rewriting History](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History))

To set a default value for a column in PostgreSQL using ALTER TABLE, use the `ALTER COLUMN ... SET DEFAULT` syntax with the column name and desired default value ([Set/Remove Default Value of Column in PostgreSQL](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default)). The new default value will only apply to subsequent INSERT or UPDATE commands and does not affect existing rows in the table ([ALTER TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html)).

## Basic Syntax

- The general form is `ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name SET DEFAULT value;` ([Set/Remove Default Value of Column in PostgreSQL](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default))
- Example: `ALTER TABLE employee ALTER COLUMN salary SET DEFAULT 0;` sets the default salary to 0 for future inserts ([Set/Remove Default Value of Column in PostgreSQL](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default))

## Removing and Expressions

- To remove an existing default value, use `DROP DEFAULT`: `ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name DROP DEFAULT;` ([Set/Remove Default Value of Column in PostgreSQL](https://www.tutorialsteacher.com/postgresql/alter-column-default))
- The default value can be an expression evaluated at insertion time, such as `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` for timestamps or `nextval('sequence_name')` for auto-incrementing values ([Default Values](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-default.html))

To pin a GitHub Action to a commit SHA in your workflow, replace the version tag with the full-length commit SHA in the `uses` statement. [Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/) and [Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security: Everything You Should Know](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide) explain how to find and apply commit SHAs for security and consistency.

## Syntax and Format

- Instead of `uses: actions/checkout@v4`, use `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683` with the full commit SHA ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).
- Include a trailing comment like `# v4.2.2` to keep the version human-readable, though it has no effect on execution ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

## Finding the Commit SHA

- Navigate to the action's repository on GitHub (e.g., https://github.com/actions/checkout for `actions/checkout`) and click the *Releases* link ([Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)).
- Copy the commit SHA from the release page—it's the long alphanumeric string that uniquely identifies that specific code version ([Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)).

## Keeping Pinned Actions Updated

- Use Dependabot to automatically update pinned commit SHAs when new versions are released by adding a `.github/dependabot.yml` configuration file ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).
- Configure Dependabot with the `github-actions` package ecosystem to receive pull requests that update both the SHA and version comment together ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

## Why Pinning Matters

- Commit SHAs are immutable: once a commit exists in Git, its SHA cannot change without altering its content, providing security against supply chain attacks ([Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)).
- GitHub's organization-level SHA pinning policy can now mandate full commit SHA pinning across all repositories, blocking workflows that use mutable tag references ([Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)).

Sources:
1. [Pinning GitHub Actions to Commit SHAs: A Practical Security Step](https://www.romainlespinasse.dev/posts/github-actions-commit-sha-pinning/)
2. [Pinning GitHub Actions for Enhanced Security: Everything You Should Know](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/pinning-github-actions-for-enhanced-security-a-complete-guide)

To build only one stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile, use the `docker build --target` flag to specify which stage to build. For example, `docker build --target build -t myapp:build .` builds only the stage named `build` and makes it the result image, instead of building all stages and producing the final one.

## Using the --target flag

- Name your stages with `FROM <image> AS <name>` in the Dockerfile, then reference that name with `--target <name>` ([Multi-Stage Build Syntax Reference](https://dockerbuild.com/reference/multi-stage-builds)).
- You can reference stages by name or by zero-based index: `docker build --target 0` builds the first stage, or `docker build --target build` builds the stage named `build` ([Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).
- If the stage name doesn't exist, the build fails with an error ([Multi-Stage Build Syntax Reference](https://dockerbuild.com/reference/multi-stage-builds)).

## BuildKit efficiency

- BuildKit (the default in Docker Desktop and Docker Engine 23.0+) only builds the target stage and its dependencies, skipping unrelated stages ([Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).
- The legacy builder (`DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0`) builds all stages sequentially up to the target, even if they aren't needed ([Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).

## Common use cases

- Debugging a specific build stage or creating a `debug` stage separate from a lean `production` stage ([Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).
- Creating a `testing` stage with test data that isn't included in the production build ([Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)).

Sources:
1. [Multi-Stage Build Syntax Reference](https://dockerbuild.com/reference/multi-stage-builds)
2. [Multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)

There are two main approaches to make Node.js automatically restart your script when files change: using the popular third-party tool Nodemon, or using Node.js's built-in native file watching feature.

## Using Nodemon (Third-Party Tool)

- [Nodemon](https://nodemon.io/) is a widely-used utility depended on by over 3 million projects that monitors your source code and automatically restarts your server when changes are detected. To use it, install it globally with `npm install -g nodemon`, then swap `nodemon` in place of `node` to run your code. Nodemon provides comprehensive features including automatic restarting, default file extension detection, support for ignoring specific files or directories, and the ability to watch specific directories ([Nodemon](https://nodemon.io/)).

## Using Native Node.js File Watching (Built-in)

- Node.js provides a built-in `--watch` flag for file monitoring without external dependencies. This feature was introduced in [Node.js version 18.11.0](https://blog.openreplay.com/no-need-for-nodemon--native-file-watching-in-node/) as an experimental feature. To use it, run `node --watch index.js` to watch your application file, and the server will automatically restart whenever you save changes (quote: "whenever you save changes to the server.js file, the server will automatically restart, reflecting those updates instantly"). For watching specific directories, use the `--watch-path` flag: `node --watch-path=./src index.js` ([No Need For Nodemon: Native File Watching in Node.js](https://blog.openreplay.com/no-need-for-nodemon--native-file-watching-in-node/)). You can also update your `package.json` start script to include the `--watch` flag for convenience: `"start": "node --watch index.js"`.

## Comparison

- Nodemon offers more advanced features like manual restarting and extensive configuration options, but adds a dependency to your project. The native `--watch` approach is simpler, more efficient, and keeps your development environment clean, though it offers basic functionality compared to Nodemon.

Sources:
1. [Nodemon](https://nodemon.io/)
2. [Node.js version 18.11.0](https://blog.openreplay.com/no-need-for-nodemon--native-file-watching-in-node/)

Rust usa um sistema de propriedade (ownership) para gerenciar memória com segurança, sem coletores de lixo. As três regras fundamentais são: cada valor tem exatamente um proprietário; só pode haver um proprietário por vez; e quando o proprietário sai do escopo, o valor é liberado automaticamente. Quando você atribui uma `String` a outra variável, a propriedade é transferida e a variável original fica inválida — isso é chamado de "move" (movimentação) e evita erros perigosos de "double free".

## As Três Regras de Propriedade

- [Cada valor tem exatamente um proprietário](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html), uma variável que o detém.
- [Há apenas um proprietário por vez; a propriedade pode ser movida mas não compartilhada](https://rustify.rs/glossary/ownership), e quando o proprietário sai do escopo, o valor é descartado.
- [Quando a variável proprietária sai do escopo, Rust chama automaticamente a função `drop` para liberar a memória](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html).

## Por Que Strings São Movidas (Move) e Não Copiadas (Copy)

- [String armazena dados na heap e seu tamanho pode variar em tempo de execução](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html), então não pode ser copiada trivialmente como inteiros.
- [Quando você atribui `s1` a `s2`, apenas o ponteiro, comprimento e capacidade na stack são copiados, não os dados da heap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html). Para prevenir erros de "double free" (liberar memória duas vezes), Rust invalida `s1`.
- [Tipos com tamanho fixo e conhecido em tempo de compilação implementam o trait `Copy` e são copiados em vez de movidos](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html), mantendo ambas as variáveis válidas.

## Move vs Clone

- [Se você realmente precisa de dois proprietários independentes, use `.clone()` para fazer uma cópia profunda explícita dos dados da heap](https://rustify.rs/glossary/ownership).
- [O sistema de propriedade elimina erros de "double free" que são comuns em linguagens como C++](https://rustify.rs/glossary/ownership), e garante memória segura com desempenho zero-cost.

Sources:
1. [Cada valor tem exatamente um proprietário](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)
2. [Há apenas um proprietário por vez; a propriedade pode ser movida mas não compartilhada](https://rustify.rs/glossary/ownership)

judge.rationale: A resposta apresenta todas as três regras de ownership, explica corretamente o move de String para evitar double free e distingue tipos Copy, que mantêm a variável original válida.

O tratamento de erros com `Result` em Rust oferece três abordagens principais: `unwrap`, `expect` e o operador `?`, cada uma com um propósito diferente na propagação e manipulação de erros.

## O tipo Result e seus métodos

- [`Result<T, E>`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/) é um enum que representa sucesso (`Ok(T)`) ou falha (`Err(E)`), forçando o programador a lidar com erros de forma explícita ([documentação oficial](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/)). O tipo é anotado com `#[must_use]`, garantindo que o compilador avise quando um Result é ignorado.

## Unwrap vs Expect: extração com panics

- **`unwrap()`** panics com uma mensagem genérica do sistema. Use quando tiver certeza absoluta de que o valor é `Ok` ou em testes ([DEV Community](https://dev.to/ssivakumar/rust-expect-vs-unwrap-vs--o7k)).
- **`expect("mensagem")`** panics com uma mensagem customizada que você fornece, facilitando o debug. Use quando quiser deixar claro por que espera sucesso ([documentação oficial](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/))e em código não-trivial.

## O operador ?: propagação de erros

- O operador `?` simplifica a propagação de erros para a função chamadora, eliminando boilerplate. Quando aplicado a um `Result`, retorna o valor `Ok` desembrulhado ou retorna o `Err` imediatamente da função atual ([documentação oficial](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/)) (quote: "Ending the expression with ? will result in the Ok's unwrapped value, unless the result is Err, in which case Err is returned early from the enclosing function"). Exemplo comparativo: sem `?` você precisa fazer `if let Err(e) = resultado { return Err(e) }` para cada chamada; com `?` é apenas `resultado?` ([DEV Community](https://dev.to/ssivakumar/rust-expect-vs-unwrap-vs--o7k)).

## Alternativas: unwrap_or e composição

- Para evitar panics, use [`unwrap_or(valor_padrao)`](https://rustlang.com.br/receitas/tratar-erros/) para fornecer um padrão fixo ou `unwrap_or_else(closure)` para calcular um valor padrão dinamicamente ([Rust Brasil](https://rustlang.com.br/receitas/tratar-erros/)). Combinadores como `map()`, `and_then()` e `map_err()` permitem transformar valores e erros sem panicking.

Sources:
1. [`Result<T, E>`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/result/)
2. [DEV Community](https://dev.to/ssivakumar/rust-expect-vs-unwrap-vs--o7k)
3. [`unwrap_or(valor_padrao)`](https://rustlang.com.br/receitas/tratar-erros/) (unsupported: the cited page does not contain the quoted text)

Em JavaScript, `var`, `let` e `const` diferem fundamentalmente em escopo, hoisting e reatribuição. `var` possui escopo de função, é inicializado como `undefined` durante hoisting e permite reatribuição e redeclaração. `let` e `const` possuem escopo de bloco, não são inicializados durante hoisting (criando a Temporal Dead Zone) e não permitem redeclaração, mas `const` não permite reatribuição após inicialização.

## Escopo

- `var` tem escopo de função ou global: escapa de blocos `if`, `for` e `{}` ([let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var))
- `let` e `const` têm escopo de bloco: confinados ao par de chaves `{}` mais próximo ([JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp))
- Em loops clássicos, `var` cria uma única vinculação compartilhada, enquanto `let` cria uma vinculação nova a cada iteração ([let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var))

## Hoisting

- `var` é hoisted e inicializado como `undefined` automaticamente ([JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp))
- `let` e `const` são hoisted mas permanecem não inicializados, criando a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) ([let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var))
- A TDZ é a região entre o início do escopo e a linha de declaração, onde acessar a variável causa um erro ([Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/))

## Reatribuição e Redeclaração

- `var` permite reatribuição e redeclaração na mesma escopo ([Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/))
- `let` permite reatribuição mas não redeclaração ([JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp))
- `const` congela a vinculação, não permitindo reatribuição após inicialização, embora objetos e arrays possam ter suas propriedades modificadas ([let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var))
- A prática recomendada é usar `const` por padrão, `let` quando há reatribuição genuína, e nunca usar `var` em código moderno ([let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var))

Sources:
1. [let vs const vs var: The Complete Guide](https://javascript.ac/en/guides/let-const-var)
2. [JavaScript var let and const](https://www.w3schools.com/Js/js_varletconst.asp)
3. [Difference between var, let and const keywords in JavaScript](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/)

judge.rationale: A resposta explica corretamente escopo, hoisting e reatribuição sem contradizer os nuggets, mas não afirma explicitamente que `const` deve ser inicializada no momento da declaração.

Git rebase es un comando que reescribe el historial de commits, moviendo una serie de commits de una rama a una nueva base, creando nuevos identificadores de commit y dejando un historial más lineal y limpio sin commits de fusión intermedios ([Git rebase | Tutorial de Atlassian sobre Git](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)) (quote: "La reorganización es el proceso de mover o combinar una secuencia de confirmaciones en una nueva confirmación base").

## Cómo funciona

- Git toma los commits de tu rama actual y los vuelve a aplicar sobre la base especificada, generando nuevos hashes para cada commit ([Git rebase | Tutorial de Atlassian sobre Git](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)).
- Existen dos modos: el rebase estándar que mueve automáticamente los commits, y el rebase interactivo (`git rebase -i`) que permite editar, reordenar, fusionar o eliminar commits durante el proceso ([Cómo utilizar Git Rebase paso a paso y sin liarla](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).
- El resultado es un historial donde parece que los cambios siempre se realizaron sobre la versión más actualizada de la rama base ([Git Rebase: cómo funciona y por qué deberías usarlo](https://hostman.com/es/tutorials/git-rebase-c%C3%B3mo-funciona-y-por-qu%C3%A9-deber%C3%ADas-usarlo/)).

## Cuándo NO usar rebase

- **Nunca en ramas públicas compartidas**: No debes hacer rebase en commits que ya se han enviado a un repositorio remoto donde otros desarrolladores están trabajando ([Git rebase | Tutorial de Atlassian sobre Git](https://www.atlassian.com/es/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)).
- **Evitar en equipos colaborativos sin coordinación**: Si haces rebase en una rama compartida y fuerzas el push, rompes el vínculo entre la versión remota y las versiones locales de tus compañeros, obligándoles a resincronizar con un historial diferente ([Cómo utilizar Git Rebase paso a paso y sin liarla](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).
- **Cuando hay ramas largas con muchos cambios**: El rebase commit a commit puede generar conflictos frecuentes y tedios de resolver; en estos casos, merge puede ser más práctico ([Git Rebase: cómo funciona y por qué deberías usarlo](https://hostman.com/es/tutorials/git-rebase-c%C3%B3mo-funciona-y-por-qu%C3%A9-deber%C3%ADas-usarlo/)).

## Casos seguros para usar

- Ramas de feature locales antes de compartirlas: El rebase interactivo permite limpiar y organizar los commits de tu rama personal ([Cómo utilizar Git Rebase paso a paso y sin liarla](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).
- Para sincronizar cambios de la rama principal localmente: Usar `git rebase origin/master` en tu rama local antes de hacer merge mantiene un historial lineal ([Cómo utilizar Git Rebase paso a paso y sin liarla](https://mundobytes.com/como-utilizar-git-rebase/)).

A LGPD impõe aos desenvolvedores obrigações técnicas e legais sobre direitos dos titulares, responsabilidades do encarregado, notificação de incidentes e penalidades severas por não conformidade. Entender cada aspecto é essencial para implementar privacidade por design no código.

## Direitos do titular que o desenvolvedor deve implementar

- **Acesso e portabilidade:** Endpoint `/api/me/data-export` deve retornar todos os dados pessoais em formato legível (JSON, CSV) com prazo legal de 15 dias para resposta ([LGPD para desenvolvedores: o que você precisa implementar](https://www.nuptechs.com/blog/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores)).
- **Revogação de consentimento:** Deve ser tão fácil revogar quanto foi consentir; o sistema deve registrar em tabela `user_consents` quando o consentimento foi concedido, revogado, IP e user agent, e interromper imediatamente o tratamento de dados ([LGPD para Desenvolvedores](https://icardb.com/artigos/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores)).
- **Deleção e anonimização:** Soft delete com anonimização é preferível a DELETE para integridade referencial; dados com obrigação legal (ex: notas fiscais por 5 anos) devem ser anonimizados mas retidos ([LGPD para desenvolvedores: o que você precisa implementar](https://www.nuptechs.com/blog/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores)).

## Obrigações do encarregado (DPO)

- **Comunicação de incidentes:** O encarregado ou representante legalmente constituído do controlador deve comunicar à ANPD através do sistema SEI! em até 3 dias úteis, contendo: descrição dos dados afetados, categorias e quantidade de titulares, riscos relacionados, medidas técnicas de segurança utilizadas, e medidas de mitigação adotadas ([Comunicação de Incidente de Segurança - ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br/canais_atendimento/agente-de-tratamento/comunicado-de-incidente-de-seguranca-cis)).
- **Notificação aos titulares:** Deve ser feita "de forma individual e diretamente aos titulares, sempre que possível" em linguagem simples, indicando os dados violados, possíveis impactos, medidas adotadas e contato do encarregado ([Comunicação de Incidente de Segurança - ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br/canais_atendimento/agente-de-tratamento/comunicado-de-incidente-de-seguranca-cis)).

## Incidentes de segurança: detecção, contenção e comunicação

- **Detecção automática:** Implementar alertas para acesso massivo a dados pessoais, export acima do volume normal, tentativas de login anômalas, e queries incomuns no banco; dashboard de segurança com métricas de logins falhados, acessos a dados sensíveis, volume exportado ([LGPD para desenvolvedores: o que você precisa implementar](https://www.nuptechs.com/blog/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores)).
- **Avaliação de risco:** Considerar o contexto da atividade, categorias e quantidades de titulares afetados, natureza dos dados, danos potenciais (materiais, morais, reputacionais), se os dados estavam criptografados, e se medidas de mitigação foram suficientes ([Comunicação de Incidente de Segurança - ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br/canais_atendimento/agente-de-tratamento/comunicado-de-incidente-de-seguranca-cis)).
- **Comunicação preliminar e complementar:** Se informações não estiverem disponíveis no prazo, pode-se comunicar preliminarmente e complementar em até 20 dias úteis, desde que devidamente justificado ([Comunicação de Incidente de Segurança - ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br/canais_atendimento/agente-de-tratamento/comunicado-de-incidente-de-seguranca-cis)).

## Multas e penalidades por não conformidade

- **Cálculo da multa:** A ANPD usa Regulamento de Dosimetria (Resolução CD/ANPD Nº 4/2023) em quatro etapas: enquadra a infração em leve, médio ou grave, calcula multa base sobre percentual da receita bruta, aplica circunstâncias agravantes (reincidência +10% até 40%, dano a grupos vulneráveis, alto volume, vantagem econômica obtida) e atenuantes (cessação voluntária, cooperação, ausência de histórico, adoção de políticas de boa-fé), e ajusta para proporcionalidade ([As multas da LGPD](https://confidata.com.br/blog/multas-lgpd-valores-criterios-casos)).
- **Multiplicidade de infrações:** Cada infração identificada gera multa separada; três infrações podem resultar em até R$ 150 milhões em multas acumuladas ([As multas da LGPD](https://confidata.com.br/blog/multas-lgpd-valores-criterios-casos)).
- **Fatores atenuantes:** Documentar inventário de dados (ROPA), encarregado nomeado, canal de atendimento a titulares, treinamento documentado, plano de resposta a incidentes, contratos com operadores (DPAs) e cooperação com investigações reduzem o valor das sanções ([As multas da LGPD](https://confidata.com.br/blog/multas-lgpd-valores-criterios-casos)).
- **Intensificação da fiscalização:** A ANPD publicou Mapa de Temas Prioritários 2026-2027 com 75 ações de fiscalização focando dados biométricos, saúde, financeiros, crianças/adolescentes e inteligência artificial; a fase educativa está encerrando e a fase de responsabilização está começando ([As multas da LGPD](https://confidata.com.br/blog/multas-lgpd-valores-criterios-casos)).

Sources:
1. [LGPD para Desenvolvedores: Privacidade por Design](https://icardb.com/artigos/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores) (partial: a number or identifier in the claim is not on the cited page)
2. [LGPD para desenvolvedores: o que você precisa implementar](https://www.nuptechs.com/blog/lgpd-para-desenvolvedores)
3. [Comunicação de Incidente de Segurança - ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br/canais_atendimento/agente-de-tratamento/comunicado-de-incidente-de-seguranca-cis)
4. [As multas da LGPD](https://confidata.com.br/blog/multas-lgpd-valores-criterios-casos)

judge.rationale: A resposta aborda o tema, mas não afirma integralmente nenhum dos fatos de referência, omitindo requisitos essenciais sobre confirmação do tratamento, correção, nomeação e divulgação do encarregado, limiar de risco do incidente e multa de 2% limitada a R$ 50 milhões por infração.

Uma expressão de agendamento no crontab consiste em cinco campos de tempo seguidos pelo comando a executar, onde cada campo representa uma unidade de tempo e todos os cinco devem corresponder simultaneamente para disparar o trabalho. [Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)

## Os cinco campos e seus intervalos

- **Minuto** (0-59): define o minuto da hora em que o comando será executado[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- **Hora** (0-23): define a hora do dia usando formato 24 horas[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- **Dia do mês** (1-31): define qual dia do mês o comando será executado[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- **Mês** (1-12 ou JAN-DEC): define qual mês; pode usar números ou abreviações de três letras[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- **Dia da semana** (0-7 ou SUN-SAT): define qual dia da semana; tanto 0 quanto 7 representam domingo[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)

## Atalhos especiais (@reboot, @daily e outros)

- `@reboot`: executa uma única vez na inicialização do daemon cron[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- `@daily` (equivalente a `0 0 * * *`): executa uma vez por dia à meia-noite[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- `@hourly` (equivalente a `0 * * * *`): executa uma vez por hora no minuto 0[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- `@weekly` (equivalente a `0 0 * * 0`): executa uma vez por semana à meia-noite de domingo[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- `@monthly` (equivalente a `0 0 1 * *`): executa uma vez por mês à meia-noite do primeiro dia[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- `@yearly` e `@annually` (equivalente a `0 0 1 1 *`): executam uma vez por ano à meia-noite de 1º de janeiro[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)

## Operadores especiais para construir intervalos

- Asterisco (`*`): corresponde a todos os valores válidos do campo[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- Barra (`/`): define intervalos; `*/5` no campo de minutos dispara a cada 5 minutos[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- Hífen (`-`): define um intervalo contínuo; `9-17` na hora dispara de 9 AM a 5 PM[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)
- Vírgula (`,`): separa valores discretos; `1,3,5` no dia da semana dispara segunda, quarta e sexta[Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)

Sources:
1. [Crontab Syntax Explained: The Complete Time Format Guide](https://benzhub.github.io/en/post/linux/024-crontab-syntax/)

judge.rationale: A afirmação de que todos os cinco campos devem corresponder simultaneamente contradiz a regra de que, quando dia do mês e dia da semana são restritos, basta um deles corresponder.

Tokio is actively maintained and is the clear winner; async-std was officially discontinued on August 24, 2025. While both are robust runtimes for Rust async programming, they differ significantly in architecture, ecosystem support, and long-term viability.

## Maintenance and Adoption

- Tokio remains actively maintained with the latest stable version 1.48.0 (as of late 2025) and receives frequent updates and bug fixes ([Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)). Tokio dominates adoption with 58 million total downloads and 26,400 GitHub stars versus async-std's 12 million downloads and 3,900 stars ([tokio vs async-std](https://generalistprogrammer.com/comparisons/tokio-vs-async-std)).
- Async-std was discontinued and is no longer updated, with its last stable version being 1.10.0 released on August 24, 2025 ([Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)) (quote: "Last stable version (2025): 1.10.0 (discontinued, 2025-08-24)"). For production systems requiring long-term support, tokio is now the only viable choice ([Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)).

## Architecture and Performance

- Tokio uses a multi-threaded runtime with a work-stealing task scheduler that scales across CPU cores, while async-std employs a single-threaded model with a thread pool ([Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)). In benchmarks, async-std achieves approximately 250k I/O-bound operations per second with 1.2% idle CPU usage and 30MB memory footprint, while Tokio reaches around 200k operations with 2.1% idle CPU and 50MB memory, though Tokio excels in high-concurrency scenarios ([Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)).

## API Design and Ecosystem

- Async-std provides APIs that mirror the Rust standard library more closely, making it easier for beginners to learn async programming, while tokio introduces more complex abstractions for advanced control ([tokio vs async-std](https://generalistprogrammer.com/comparisons/tokio-vs-async-std)) (quote: "async-std provides APIs that mirror std library more closely for easier learning; Tokio has multi-threaded and current-thread runtimes, async-std focuses on simplicity"). Tokio has a vastly larger ecosystem with mature libraries like Hyper (HTTP), Tonic (gRPC), Tower (networking), and numerous database drivers, whereas async-std has limited third-party support ([tokio vs async-std](https://generalistprogrammer.com/comparisons/tokio-vs-async-std)).

Sources:
1. [Rust Async Programming: Tokio, async-std, and Patterns](https://dasroot.net/posts/2025/12/rust-async-programming-tokio-async-std-patterns/)
2. [tokio vs async-std](https://generalistprogrammer.com/comparisons/tokio-vs-async-std)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly identifies Tokio as maintained and async-std as discontinued, describes Tokio’s work-stealing scheduler, and gives a broadly relevant comparison without directly contradicting the reference facts, though it omits smol, async-compat, and Tokio’s MSRV and states the std-interface point too vaguely.

Use `Rc` for single-threaded shared ownership with minimal overhead, and `Arc` for thread-safe shared ownership across multiple threads. The key difference is that `Arc` uses atomic operations for reference counting, making it thread-safe but slightly slower, while `Rc` uses non-atomic operations and cannot be sent between threads.

## Core Differences

- `Rc` (Reference Counted) is single-threaded and uses non-atomic reference counting, making it faster with lower overhead ([std::rc - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/)).
- `Arc` (Atomically Reference Counted) is thread-safe and uses atomic operations to manage reference counts across threads ([std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)).
- Both occupy the same amount of memory; the only difference is how they update the reference count ([Choosing Rc vs Arc for Shared Ownership in Different Contexts](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-rc-vs-arc-for-shared-ownership-in-different-contexts/)).

## When to Use Each

- Use `Rc` in single-threaded contexts where shared ownership is confined within one thread, since it avoids the performance cost of atomic operations ([Choosing Rc vs Arc for Shared Ownership in Different Contexts](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-rc-vs-arc-for-shared-ownership-in-different-contexts/)).
- Use `Arc` whenever your data is shared across multiple threads, as it provides thread-safe reference counting ([std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)).
- The compiler enforces this at compile time: attempting to send an `Rc` between threads will fail to compile, so `Rc` is a safe default for single-threaded code ([std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)).

Sources:
1. [std::rc - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/)
2. [std::sync - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)
3. [Choosing Rc vs Arc for Shared Ownership in Different Contexts](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-rc-vs-arc-for-shared-ownership-in-different-contexts/)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains the Rc-versus-Arc choice and atomic-overhead tradeoff without contradicting the nuggets, but it does not state that Rc is also !Sync or that Arc<T> is Send and Sync only when T is Send and Sync.

PostgreSQL offers two JSON data types with distinct storage and performance characteristics: `json` stores the original input text exactly as provided, while `jsonb` stores data in a decomposed binary format for faster processing and indexing.

## Storage and Processing

- `json` preserves the exact input text, including whitespace, key ordering, and duplicate keys, but must reparse the entire field on each operation ([PostgreSQL JSON Types documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))
- `jsonb` stores data in a binary format that is slightly slower to insert due to conversion overhead, but significantly faster to process since no reparsing is needed ([PostgreSQL JSON Types documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))

## Indexing and Advanced Features

- `jsonb` supports GIN indexes for efficient searching of keys and key/value pairs across large numbers of documents, while `json` does not support direct indexing ([PostgreSQL JSON Types documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))
- `jsonb` includes containment operators (`@>`), existence operators (`?`), and many additional JSON-specific functions that `json` lacks ([DbVisualizer - JSON vs JSONB](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/))

## When to Use Each Type

- Use `json` for write-heavy workloads like logging where you perform many inserts and do not need complex queries, and when preserving exact JSON formatting is important ([DbVisualizer - JSON vs JSONB](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/))
- Use `jsonb` for dynamic data that requires updates, querying, and indexing—most modern applications should prefer `jsonb` unless there are specialized legacy requirements ([PostgreSQL JSON Types documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html))

Sources:
1. [PostgreSQL JSON Types documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)
2. [DbVisualizer - JSON vs JSONB](https://www.dbvis.com/thetable/json-vs-jsonb-in-postgresql-a-complete-comparison/) (unsupported: the cited page does not contain the quoted text)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains the core storage, processing, indexing, and usage differences without contradiction, but it does not explicitly state that jsonb discards whitespace and key order or keeps only the last duplicate key.

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ fundamentally in their transport layer and header compression mechanisms. HTTP/2 runs over TCP with HPACK header compression, while HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) with QPACK, addressing TCP's head-of-line blocking problem and enabling connection migration.

## Transport Protocol

- HTTP/2 uses TCP, which guarantees ordered delivery of a single byte stream, meaning any lost packet stalls all requests on the connection until retransmission completes ([HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: TCP, QUIC and Fallback](https://howhttpworks.com/compare/http2-vs-http3)).
- HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, which tracks ordering per stream independently, so a lost packet only blocks the affected streams while other streams continue ([HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: TCP, QUIC and Fallback](https://howhttpworks.com/compare/http2-vs-http3)).
- QUIC combines cryptographic and transport handshakes into one, reducing connection establishment time compared to TCP's separate three-way handshake and TLS negotiation ([HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction)).

## Header Compression

- HTTP/2 uses HPACK (RFC 7541), which maintains synchronized dynamic tables on encoder and decoder that reference headers by index, relying on TCP's in-order delivery guarantee ([HPACK vs QPACK: HTTP Header Compression Compared](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack)).
- HTTP/3 uses QPACK (RFC 9204), which solves the out-of-order delivery problem of QUIC by using dedicated encoder and decoder streams with acknowledgments, allowing the decoder to wait for dynamic table entries or use literal representations to avoid blocking ([HPACK vs QPACK: HTTP Header Compression Compared](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack)).
- Both HPACK and QPACK achieve similar compression ratios in practice, typically 85–95% reduction in header size, with QPACK's overhead from separate streams being minimal ([HPACK vs QPACK: HTTP Header Compression Compared](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack)).

## Additional Transport Benefits

- QUIC enables connection migration using connection IDs instead of IP addresses, allowing clients to maintain the same connection when switching between Wi-Fi and cellular networks, whereas TCP connections break on address changes ([HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: TCP, QUIC and Fallback](https://howhttpworks.com/compare/http2-vs-http3)).

Sources:
1. [HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: TCP, QUIC and Fallback](https://howhttpworks.com/compare/http2-vs-http3)
2. [HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3](https://www.logicmonitor.com/deep-dive/http3-vs-http2/introduction)
3. [HPACK vs QPACK: HTTP Header Compression Compared](https://www.dev-toolbox.tech/tools/http-protocol-comparison/examples/hpack-vs-qpack)

judge.rationale: The answer correctly explains HTTP/2 over TCP with HPACK and HTTP/3 over QUIC with QPACK, but does not explicitly state that QPACK's dedicated streams are unidirectional or cover ALPN/Alt-Svc discovery, TCP fallback, or HTTP/2 binary multiplexed framing.

Git merge and rebase are both ways to integrate changes from one branch into another, but they handle history differently. Merge creates a new commit that ties together the histories of both branches, while rebase rewrites commits by moving them on top of another branch's tip, creating a linear history.

## How they integrate branches

- **Merge** creates a non-destructive merge commit that explicitly captures when one branch was integrated into another, preserving the complete history of both branches ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))
- **Rebase** rewrites project history by moving an entire branch to the tip of another, resulting in a linear history without merge commits ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))

## When to avoid rebase

- **Never rebase public branches** that others are working on or have pulled. The golden rule is: "Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and people may have based work on them." Rebasing creates new commits that diverge from the originals, forcing other developers to reconcile conflicting histories ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))
- **Avoid rebasing after creating a pull request**, as other developers will then be reviewing your commits and rewriting history makes it impossible to track follow-up changes ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))
- **Don't force-push rebased branches** to shared repositories unless certain no one else is working on those commits. Force-pushing rewrites the remote history and confuses collaborators ([When to Avoid Git Rebase - Java Code Geeks](https://www.javacodegeeks.com/2024/03/when-to-avoid-git-rebase.html))

- **Local cleanup** before pushing: use interactive rebase on unpushed commits to squash, reorder, or edit commits without affecting others ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))
- **Incorporate upstream changes into a private feature branch** by rebasing onto the main branch tip, then merge the feature into main once approved, ensuring a linear history ([Merging vs. rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing))

Lists and tuples are both Python sequence types, but the fundamental difference is mutability: lists are mutable (changeable after creation) while tuples are immutable (fixed once created). This distinction determines their performance characteristics and appropriate use cases.

## Mutability

- [Lists are mutable](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/), allowing you to add, remove, or modify elements after creation using methods like `append()`, `remove()`, and `extend()`.
- [Tuples are immutable](https://dev.to/beatrisilieva/python-lists-vs-tuples-mutable-vs-immutable-data-structures-and-when-to-use-each-3790), so once created they cannot be changed; any attempt to modify elements raises a TypeError.
- [If a tuple contains mutable objects like lists, those inner objects can still be modified](https://dev.to/beatrisilieva/python-lists-vs-tuples-mutable-vs-immutable-data-structures-and-when-to-use-each-3790), but the tuple's structure itself remains fixed.

## Performance and Memory

- [Tuples consume less memory than lists](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/) because they are immutable and don't require extra space for dynamic resizing.
- [Tuples are faster to iterate over](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/) since their immutability allows Python to store them in contiguous memory and apply optimizations.

## Typical Use Cases

- [Use lists for collections that need to change](https://pytutorial.com/python-lists-vs-tuples-key-differences-explained/), such as to-do lists, shopping lists, or any data you need to dynamically modify, sort, or filter.
- [Use tuples for fixed data that should not change](https://pytutorial.com/python-lists-vs-tuples-key-differences-explained/), such as geographic coordinates, color values, or dictionary keys, and to communicate intent that data is constant.
- [Tuples can serve as dictionary keys because they are hashable](https://pytutorial.com/python-lists-vs-tuples-key-differences-explained/) while lists cannot.

Sources:
1. [Lists are mutable](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/python-difference-between-list-and-tuple/)
2. [Tuples are immutable](https://dev.to/beatrisilieva/python-lists-vs-tuples-mutable-vs-immutable-data-structures-and-when-to-use-each-3790)
3. [Use lists for collections that need to change](https://pytutorial.com/python-lists-vs-tuples-key-differences-explained/)

HashMap provides O(1) average-case lookups with unordered keys, while BTreeMap offers O(log n) access with keys automatically kept in sorted order. Choose HashMap for speed-critical applications where ordering doesn't matter, and BTreeMap when you need sorted iteration, range queries, or deterministic ordering.

## Key Requirements

- HashMap keys must implement `Hash` and `Eq` traits, typically derived with `#[derive(Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]` ([HashMap in std::collections - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html)).
- BTreeMap keys must implement `Ord` trait for total ordering, derived with `#[derive(Ord, PartialOrd, Eq, PartialEq)]` ([BTreeMap in std::collections - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/collections/struct.BTreeMap.html)).
- Floating-point keys (`f64`, `f32`) cannot be used in either map: `f64` does not implement `Ord` or `Hash` because NaN breaks total ordering and equality semantics ([What Is the Difference Between HashMap and BTreeMap in Rust?](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/what-is-the-difference-between-hashmap-and-btreemap-in-rust/)).

## Ordering and Iteration

- HashMap iterates in arbitrary order with no guarantees, and iteration order may differ between program runs due to random seeding ([HashMap in std::collections - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html)).
- BTreeMap always iterates in sorted key order, with operations like `iter()`, `keys()`, and `values()` producing items in key order ([BTreeMap in std::collections - Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/collections/struct.BTreeMap.html)).
- BTreeMap enables efficient range queries via `range()` method in O(log n + k) time, where k is result count; HashMap requires linear O(n) iteration to filter results ([What Is the Difference Between HashMap and BTreeMap in Rust?](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/what-is-the-difference-between-hashmap-and-btreemap-in-rust/)).

## When to Choose Each

- Use HashMap for high-performance lookups and insertion when ordering is irrelevant, memory efficiency isn't critical, and random access dominates your workload ([Rust - Choosing HashMap vs BTreeMap: Trade-offs in performance and ordering](https://www.slingacademy.com/article/choosing-hashmap-vs-btreemap-trade-offs-in-performance-and-ordering/)).
- Use BTreeMap when you need sorted iteration, range queries, deterministic serialization, or when keys only implement `Ord` and not `Hash`; it can also outperform HashMap on full-map iteration due to better cache locality ([What Is the Difference Between HashMap and BTreeMap in Rust?](https://www.rustfaq.org/en/what-is-the-difference-between-hashmap-and-btreemap-in-rust/)).

Rust's Mutex and RwLock are both synchronization primitives for protecting shared data, but they differ fundamentally in their locking strategy and poisoning behavior. Mutex enforces exclusive access to one thread at a time, while RwLock allows multiple concurrent readers or one exclusive writer, making it more efficient for read-heavy workloads.

## Locking mechanisms

- Mutex blocks any thread waiting for access, treating all threads equally whether they read or write ([std::sync::Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)).
- RwLock allows multiple readers to hold the lock simultaneously as long as no writer is present, while write access remains exclusive ([std::sync::RwLock](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)).
- This concurrent read capability makes RwLock more performant for workloads with frequent reads and infrequent writes ([Rust Read-Write Locks](https://medium.com/@TechSavvyScribe/rust-read-write-locks-managing-concurrent-read-and-write-access-a6ab689bbed3)).

## Poisoning behavior

- Both Mutex and RwLock implement poisoning: when a thread holding the lock panics, the lock becomes poisoned and subsequent lock attempts return an error ([std::sync::Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)).
- RwLock differs critically: it only poisons on panic during write (exclusive) access, not during read operations ([std::sync::RwLock](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)).
- Both support recovery from poisoning via `into_inner()` on the `PoisonError` or by using `clear_poison()` to manually reset the poisoned state ([std::sync::Mutex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Mutex.html)).

2. [std::sync::RwLock](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html)
3. [Rust Read-Write Locks](https://medium.com/@TechSavvyScribe/rust-read-write-locks-managing-concurrent-read-and-write-access-a6ab689bbed3)
